subtopic: PETITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, within the boundaries of Metro Toronto and the city of Scarborough, Canadians have a rare opportunity for a major environmental issue. That issue is to establish a Rouge River Valley system to be a preserved and protected area for all generations.
The Rouge River is a unique and precious natural area. It has significant archaeological sites within the valley that date back many thousands of years. The whole 5,000 acres of this land is being threatened by the discussions of the Metro Toronto Council of pursuing this as a garbage dump site. It is threatened as well by the Government of the Province of Ontario, who wish to build a major freeway right up through the middle of this particularly beautiful valley.
The constituents of Scarborough Centre, people in Metro Toronto and Canadians right across the country are really outraged with both of these discussions taking place.
They call upon the Government of Canada in the national interest, to join with the mayor of Scarborough, the federal Minister of the Environment for the Government of Canada, and the coalition of Scarborough community associations to have the Rouge River Valley preserved as a Canadian heritage land or a provincial park.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the motion we have moved is one which has the full support of the New Democratic caucus. It is also one which demands the support of everyone in the House.
Supply
What we are doing is reaffirming the Government's pledge. We want the House to stand behind the Government so that all Canadians and all of the people directly involved, even internationally, will know how we feel about this resolution which can have ramifications far beyond the people directly involved. It could affect the whole of Canada and could even affect others as well. We welcome, ask and hope for the support of all Members in the House.
The issue arose from the U.S. challenge to GATT of West Coast fishing regulations which required West Coast salmon and herring to be landed in British Columbia to be processed. To be processed means landing, counting, eviscerating and grading. That is what the regulations required. These were challenged by the U.S. before GATT.
We need these regulations in B.C. to protect our market. It is an important market. Eighty per cent of that product is exported from B.C. and from Canada. We get top prices because we have been able to guarantee the quantities we promised. We have been able to guarantee the quality of our product better than any other supplier in the world. We need those regulations to protect our resource.
We are talking about five species of salmon and in excess of 1,200 separate races of salmon. To be able to protect each individual race, we have to protect the environment. When we are talking about the environment, we are talking about drift nets which are operating some thousands of miles out to sea and raiding our salmon resource. We are talking about a point as far distant from that as one in excess of 1,000 miles upstream in some cases, where some of the salmon spawn. All of that environment needs protection because we have to be able to ensure adequate escapement for each of the 1,200 races. We need that to protect the supply for the processors in British Columbia who have some $600 million invested in the processing industry. They have invested that, secure in the knowledge that they had control of the supply. They are constantly upgrading, rebuilding, and carrying on a continuing program of research and development to maintain Canada's standards of quality salmon being shipped to international markets.
We need the supply to protect the livelihood of some 19,500 people in the Province of British Columbia who work in the fishing industry. These are the Minister's own figures. There are some 8,000 shore workers and

June 15, 1989
Supply
11,500 fishermen on gill-netters, seiners, and trailers. We need the supply so that they may catch it and maintain their livelihoods.
On the East Coast there are some 90,000 people working in the fishing industry at all levels. They need the supply on the East Coast just as much as we need it on the West.
We need the employment. We need to add value to what, by international agreement, is a Canadian resource. Everyone has agreed that salmon coming down our rivers going out to sea and coming back, wherever they are in the world, belong to British Columbia if that is where they came from to begin with.
We want to be able to add value to that resource. It is important to the many small coastal communities of British Columbia. It is the life-blood of many of these communities. Without processing, they will simply die. It is important because it provides the only alternative to today's social assistance, yesterday's social welfare or relief. We abandoned those naughty words and now call it social assistance. Whatever it is, it is a totally demeaning existence for thousands of women in particular, especially native women, whose only opportunity to get away from social assistance is to work in the canneries operating on the B.C. coast.
We have discussed the American threat under GATT, and it has been said that the New Democrats are strong supporters of GATT. Indeed we are. We all believe in trade, especially for Canada, since we are a very strong trading nation. We have to believe in trade for the B.C. fish. We export 80 per cent of our fish products, and we do not want to stop that or interfere with it in any way. Indeed, we would like to build on that, to increase it, and to continue to improve the quality of B.C. salmon. However, to abandon recklessly our right to process our own resource would threaten our ability to guarantee the market supply.
We have to know what is happening. We have to be able to count and identify the species. We have to be able to identify and control the races. To guarantee our supply, we have to be able to land those fish, count them, eviscerate them, and grade them. We can only maintain
our world-wide reputation for quality if we have total control of the value added factor in Canada.
We have to protect the continued existence of the many races of salmon. It is not enough to protect just one race or even one species. We want to protect all the species and all the races. We can only do that if we know exactly what is being caught, where they are being caught, and when they are being caught. We have to be able to ensure that there is sufficient escapement of each race so that the race will survive. We want to maintain employment opportunities in Canada for the over
100,000	Canadian workers on both coasts who work in the fish processing industry.
We were told that the GATT decision cannot be appealed and we agree with that. However, we could have rejected it, as has been the practice of the United States and other signatories to GATT on many occasions. We had that option but chose not to use it.
The new regulations, relatively useless as they may be, are supposed to be GATT consistent. Why did we bow so subserviently to the American Government in abandoning our opportunity through GATT to reject that decision? Why did we not ask for a GATT ruling on the new regulations if we were determined to go that route? Why did we go instead to the Free Trade Council? If we are sure that they are GATT consistent, why not go to GATT to ask the question; why go to the Free Trade Council? Are we in danger of setting a precedent?
By knuckling under so early to the Americans, are we jeopardizing other measures such as Newfoundland's regulations that prohibit the trucking of groundfish out of Canada, similar regulations in New Brunswick and Quebec, Ontario legislation that provides for the further processing of minerals in the Province of Ontario before export, B.C. legislation that provides for the further manufacture of B.C. logs before they may be shipped out? How about the United States itself? The American Magnuson Act provides for the processing of American fish before it may be shipped out.
We have no desire to enter into any kind of a war, trade or otherwise with the United States, our best trading partner. However, continued good relations depend upon fair treatment on both sides. We are their nearest, largest, and most politically stable supplier of

raw and partially processed raw material. We want to maintain that relationship.
We have shown our good faith by entering into the Free Trade Agreement which, among other things, provides for Canada to ensure the American energy supply by promising to invest billions of dollars in developing our oil supply for the continuing benefit of our neighbours to the south. Consistent with GATT, we could have imposed an export tax, but we gave it up under the free trade deal. We control the export of and imposed a tax on the shake and shingle industry in British Columbia because it was interfering with shake and shingle production in the United States. We co-operated with the Americans and have done many things to co-operate with them. There would be no advantage to us or to them if we were to issue threats or counterthreats. Neither would there by any advantage to Canada or to the United States if we, with wanton abandonment, gave up control of our resources, most especially our renewable resources.
This is an important issue in British Columbia today. It can be an important issue for the Maritimes tomorrow and for Ontario's mining industry the day after. If we lose on this issue there will be nothing much left for Canadians other than to be hewers of wood, drawers of water, and miners of minerals. Even the oceans will be open to anyone.
This is an important issue. We should have taken a firm stand, and the opportunity still exists to do so. I invite Hon. Members to support actions taken by the Government to ensure that we do not lose out on this issue. We must not lose out because this is just the first step on the road to being nothing but hewers of wood, drawers of water, and fishermen for the world to exploit.
This is an important issue. We welcome the support of the whole House and hope that it will support the Government in its actions to ensure that we do not lose on this issue.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, what we are discussing this morning is a two-pronged question. First, does the Minister stand by his promise that he made to the west coast fishing industry when he said that, as the motion indicates, this Government would "not allow jobs, historically established, to be threatened"?
Supply
Over the years on the West Coast we have seen processing plants fall by the wayside as the industry has been rationalized, to the extent that now the processing of the fish resource is focused in just exclusive centres. The Government has said that there is no requirement to process fish in these plants but that they can be transferred elsewhere for processing.
Having made that decision, why would anyone carry on processing in Canada when one can move those processing plants to the United States where labour costs are significantly less, where the rules and regulations are less stringent, and where one would have the advantages of economies of scale to make the plants more efficient? Why would a single processing plant remain in Canada, make it impossible for the Minister to keep his promise, and see the disappearance of literally thousands of jobs on the West Coast? Would the Hon. Member respond to that question? How can we save this industry unless this Government changes its position and keeps it promise?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the B.C. salmon processing industry has a world-wide reputation for quality. Our price is high, but the world is prepared to pay that price because it knows the quality of our product. There has never been any problem with that. We have a reputation for being able to meet our market promises. If we promise to deliver a certain quantity of canned salmon or fishery products generally from British Columbia, we deliver them. We guarantee the quality and there has never been any question about that.
There is continuing upgrading in our canneries. A lot of money is being spent annually to make sure that we deliver a premium product because we know we are in competition with other countries that are shipping salmon. We have proven we can do it in British Columbia, and it can be GATT consistent. What we are doing is making sure that when the product leaves our shores it is ready for human consumption in the best condition possible in the light of the most modem technology, the most modem equipment, and the best workers in the world.

He

Therefore, this Minister when he speaks in the House today should stand up in his place and explain to Canadians how he is going to turn around the emphatic statement of Mr. Hunter before a committee of the House who said that if the Government permitted the Americans open access to our fish, those jobs and factories would be moved to the United States. subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY
speechtext: British Columbia salmon has had an international reputation for quality for years, indeed decades, Madam Speaker. It has always been important for us to maintain that reputation in world matters.If we are going to keep them, we can only do that if we have control and a guaranteed supply to the canneries operating in B.C. If the barriers are down, some of those canneries are going to move to the United States and process the product there. They will not produce as good a product because they will not have to, but it is going to make our product that much more difficult to sell on world markets.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to have an opportunity to take part in this very important debate which is being watched by many Canadians, especially British Columbians. I understand that some British Columbians are in this House today to witness this important discussion.
The motion calls upon the House to reaffirm the Government's pledge to the west coast salmon and herring industry to "not allow jobs, historically established, to be threatened" by any government response to GATT rulings.
What underlies the motion from the perspective of the New Democratic Party which has sponsored it is the suggestion that if only we could live in the old days of protectionism and keep export restrictions in place which guarantee a non-competitive fish processing industry, we could somehow guarantee jobs of the past in perpetuity into the future.
Recent history has shown that the New Democratic Party is usually wrong on these questions. I remember very well the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party standing in this House in November 1984. In decrying the economic statement of the Minister of Finance which set out the economic agenda of the Government for the past five years, the Leader of the New Democratic Party alleged that Canada would lose 150,000 jobs as a result of the initiatives which were taken and introduced at that time.
The people of Canada know better and they judged better on November 21, 1988. The NDP is using the same fear-mongering tactics in this House today and is trying to frighten people. The only way its Members can gain political support is by frightening people about the alternatives.
Instead of 150,000 jobs being destroyed, as they put it, 1.5 million jobs were created as a result of the economic initiatives of this Government. The national unemployment rate dropped from over 12 per cent to less than 8 per cent. There were major reductions, approximately a one-third reduction, in every province and in most industries in Canada.
Supply
Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party do not want to hear the truth. The truth is that the fishing industry of Canada, during the four years that I have presided over it, has seen untold prosperity, unparalleled in Canadian history. The income, the amount of employment, the emphasis on quality, and the value added processing opportunity have increased because we have an increasingly competitive fishing industry.
I picked up a brochure put out by the fishermen's union. I wish it were as true as it appears to be to the innocent reader. However, there is a statement in this brochure that says "the rescinding of these export restrictions," which I will come to in a moment, "is a complete betrayal of a competitive Canadian industry". It goes on to state: "Why does the Government refuse to protect an industry?"
Any thinking person knows that we cannot have a competitive industry if we always attempt to protect it from the realities of the world market-place. TTie reality of the fishing industry is that Canada exports 80 per cent of our products. In terms of the Atlantic industry, which is a large part of it, two-thirds of our exports go to the United States market. In the case of the Pacific industry, a large proportion goes to Japan and the European Community.
The point is that we depend on access to those export markets to guarantee the jobs that employ our fish plant workers and our fishermen. If we are not competitive in the international market-place, we will not sell fish and the industries of Atlantic and Pacific Canada will not pay wages.
Indeed, the Government is dedicated to preserving and enhancing the opportunities for employment and the quality of employment in the Canadian fishing industry. That will not be done if we cut ourselves off from access to a market, 80 per cent of it being an export market, which ensures employment for our people.
That means we cannot have it both ways. We have to sell competitively into the market-place the highest quality product of any country in the world. That means customers have to feel that they get the best value for their money when they buy Canadian. That has increasingly been the case.
We should understand the nature of world trade and the liberalization of world trade to which Canada is committed. Members of all Parties are also committed, I presume, because they prescribe to the process of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade in which Canada has been a participant for 40 years. Any country that is as export dependent as Canada knows that we cannot put up protectionist barriers to protect our industries, thereby ensuring they will be higher cost

Supply
industries, lower volume industries, less competitive industries, and still expect to have the free opportunity to export our products into other world markets. In other words, we have to play by the international rules of trade.
It is a fact of life that some years ago previous Canadian Governments decided to protect our salmon and herring processing industries by erecting export prohibitions on unprocessed sockeye and pink salmon and herring unless the roe was extracted in Canada. These were very important regulations at that time which helped the Canadian industry to become competitive. That competitiveness now does not depend in perpetuity on maintaining those protectionist barriers because these industries have grown up. They are big boys and girls now. We can compete. We do supply the best fish products available from our west coast fishery in those markets.
If this Government and this Minister did not believe that, we would not be devoting tens of millions of dollars to enhancing our salmon stocks on the West Coast. I would not have gone to Cabinet and worked to gain an increase in the budget of the Salmonid Enhancement Program of $208 million over five years with a firm commitment of that funding into our a base on into the next century, if I did not have confidence and faith in our ability to get maximum economic advantage out of the salmon producing and processing industry.
As I said earlier, the record of the last four years shows it is paying dividends. We have had the most prosperous years. Again this year we are to have a record year in terms of the runs of pink and sockeye. As I announced only yesterday in Vancouver, we will expect to have over 17 million pink and sockeye salmon caught this year. They will be processed in British Columbia. I am confident of that.
It is a fact of life that when fish are caught and landed close to the point where they are caught where there is infrastructure, in which there is a significant investment, which is modem, and which is the most competitive in the world, it would make no sense to truck it 600 miles to somewhere else. If we process it at that plant, we get the highest quality product. It will be Canadian Grade A prime product whether canned, frozen, or whatever
form, and we will get the best dollar from that product by processing in Canada.
These old regulations were found to be offensive because Canada, and in particular some processing companies on the northwest British Columbian coast, wanted to have their cake and eat it too. They wanted to go to Alaska and buy fish. This would not just be in surplus years, but in other years when the Alaskan processors did not have an adequate supply. They wanted to buy that fish by offering a higher price to Alaskan fishermen than the Alaskan processors were able to offer. Our processors in northwestern British Columbia want to go to United States waters and buy from their fishermen but in return say to the Alaskan processors that they cannot come into Canada and buy fish from our fishermen. That is clearly discriminatory and was found to be so by a panel of the General Agreement on Thriffs and Trade. If we want to export our products internationally, Canada has to play by the rules on a level playing field, and we were caught out in that case.
I could submit that the Americans would not have taken that case to the General Agreements on Tariffs and Trade had the Free Trade Agreement been in place, because we would then have had an avenue to negotiate a solution to that problem which we did not have then. We now have a mechanism to resolve such future disputes.

speechtext: I want to point out to the House that whether we are talking about salmon, herring, codfish or other species, Canada is not God's gift to the world. We are only a small producer.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
We take great pride in our salmon and herring stocks, but the fact is that we produce only 20 per cent of the world's supply of salmon and herring. That is an important point those nervous Nellies over there fail to acknowledge. Any country that wanted to buy raw fish and take it home and process it-it would be rather silly to truck it on ice for hundreds of miles-could buy five fish out of every six from somewhere else. For example, they could buy it from Alaska, from Norway, or from Iceland. They could buy herring from Atlantic Canada or

from the Nordic countries. In other words, there is ample choice in terms of supply of raw fish. Americans processors have access to five times as many American codfish and salmon as they do Canadian cod. Why would they all of a sudden come and buy fish from Canada rather than buy from their own fishermen?
One reason would be if our fishermen would sell it more cheaply. But why would our fishermen sell it more cheaply to Americans if they were getting a decent price from Canadian processors? This is a question that the New Democratic Party fails to address. By these export restrictions, our fishermen are held captive to the Canadian processing industry, and that is unfair to our fishermen. Now they fall silent because they know that the fishermen's union is split on this issue. Fishermen want and are entitled to the best price for their fish while we carefully manage, licence and allocate quotas to their benefit.
Now let us ask Members of the New Democratic Party what their position is. Should our fishermen not get a world competitive price for their fish? Why is it that the processing companies do not have to pay a competitive price? Because they have the supply guaranteed by those old export restrictions.
The point is that countries that would buy our raw fish have many other ways to buy fish. The only way they buy Canadian is if they can get it cheaper. Why would Canadian fishermen sell it more cheaply abroad if they can get the right price from Canadian processors? That represents the heart of the injustice that will be rectified by the new regulations. These will ensure that we maintain control of our herring and salmon for management and conservation reasons. Under the new regulations all West Coast species, all five species of salmon, must be landed in Canadian ports, inspected, counted, and biological samples taken, before anyone can buy this resource of Canada.

I was interested a few moments ago when the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. Reid) asked the lead speaker whether he supported this regulation. All Canadians should support such a landing requirement, including the processing sector, the fishermen's union and those organizations, and the New Democratic Party. I would like to know if Members of the New Democratic Party feel that groundfish, rockfish and other species should be required to be landed in Canadian ports. We believe this to be our right under Article 11 of the GATT and will be testing this shortly before a free trade panel.
If those Members are so immature as to suggest that we should not control our resource and manage it well by requiring it to be brought to Canadian ports, they should rise and state that they support those measures. They are attempting to say that the Government is going to relinquish control over our fishery. That is pure balderdash.
I have insisted during the whole period of the trade negotiations with the United States, that only Canadians shall be licensed to harvest fish in Canadian waters. We have steadfastly refused to allow American processing boats, buying boats or packers, if one wishes to call them that, to come into Canadian waters and take fish from our fishermen. This Government is adding to that assurance that we properly manage and conserve our resource by requiring it be brought to Canadian ports. To hear members of the Opposition, one would think they oppose that. Where is their sense of national patriotism?
The Government has done the correct thing in this matter by ensuring that Canadians receive the benefit of that resource at their point of landing where any self-respecting industry which intends to be competitive in the world market-place will have the best opportunity to process it right there. Not only to gut the fish. Members opposite want to have the guts taken out and then ship the fish away. We want them processed. We do not only want them to be stuffed into cans. We want our fish products put into TV dinners and higher value-added products such as fish cakes and restaurant meals. We want to get the maximum dollar value from our fishery resource. That adds up to employment for processing workers and for fishermen. It means they will get the best dollar for their product.

June 15, 1989

Canada cannot hide behind archaic protectionist regulations which shelter our workers from the realities of the world industrial commodity trading market.
When this Government took office Canada was eleventh among industrial nations. We were down at number eleven in terms of our competitiveness. I suspect when we see some figures soon, we will see that Canada is near the top. That is because this Government has rejuvenated Canadian industry in all sectors and expanding opportunity to add value to our natural resources.
That is why the Free Trade Agreement is so good for Canada and for the fishing industry. It removes the tariffs upon entry into the United States market which the Americans were applying to our salmon, herring, lobster and other fish products. With the removal of those tariffs, the price to the consumer in the United States goes down and we sell more, and we sell more value-added product, not more raw material.
I submit that members of the Opposition are way off base as usual. They were wrong in 1984. The Canadian people judged them wrong in 1988 in an election, and they will do so again in 1992 or 1993 because this Government has Canada on the rails to prosperity and we will stay there. We do not need pessimistic doom and gloom when Canadians are confident and optimistic about their future and the opportunities we can give to our nation.

I cannot help but regret the attitude of the Minister. The motion I moved states:
That this House reaffirms the government's pledge to the West
Coast salmon and herring industry to "not allow jobs, historically
established, to be threatened" by any government response to
GATT rulings."
I had hoped that the Government would agree with that, but it seems that the Government does not. The Minister in his response said that we are No. 11 in terms of competitive pricing. We are No. 11, and yet we never have had any problem selling our product at premium prices because we deliver the top product in the world. Why would people buy Canadian fish if they can get their own more cheaply? Because they know historically they have been getting a guaranteed and a superior product when they buy Canadian fish at top prices. We have never had any problem selling our Canadian fish.
Groundfish today are being trucked from Prince Rupert to the United States. Fish can be moved and are being moved. If you are prepared to sell without the restrictions, without the quality guarantees, without the quality reputation that we have for our fish products in British Columbia, then you can sell more cheaply if you do not really care what kind of garbage you are selling. I cannot say that much about the East Coast because I do not know it that well. But West Coast fishermen and the industry have built a world-wide reputation over decades for selling a guaranteed top quality product and for meeting the demands of the market. That has been our reputation, Madam Speaker.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY

Madam Speaker, I certainly agree with the Hon. Member. That is why our Canadian fish products sell and why we never have anything left over going to waste. It is top quality product priced competitively. That is the way it will continue to be. With or without this regulation, that is the reality. Our industries have invested in the most modem technology. They have upgraded their plants.
If the Hon. Member is saying that the only way the industry can make a big enough profit is to pay the fishermen too low a price, we do not want that. We are on the side of the fishermen and the plant workers. It is about time the NDP were, too. If what they are doing is siding with the processing industry and saying the only way that industiy can make a profit is to keep paying workers too little, we do not agree with that.
I do not agree with the mischievousness of this motion. I am confident that the public will judge this Government as having created economic growth, new jobs and a more competitive economy in this country. That certainly has been true of the fishing industry these past four years.
Never has so much income been enjoyed, so much value added, so much use made of under-utilized species as has been the case under this Government. While I may not agree with the mischievous language of the motion which tries to protect archaic jobs in the form that was appropriate 20, 30 or 40 years ago, I can say with confidence to this House that there will be more employment, more rewarding and year-round jobs, not jobs that put people on unemployment insurance for six months of the year. This is a result of the competitive drive of this
June 15, 1989

Government to extract more value from our natural resources, to modernize our industry and to export more product.
The Hon. Member said our fishing industry has produced the best quality product. It is bought because of its high quality. It is not bought because of the protectionist regulation that was removed. We will have an opportunity to do more of that processing when all the fish is brought to shore.
The Hon. Member has not told me why they would support the old regulations which did not require that coho, chinook or chum salmon be brought to shore. They do not want that fish protected. We are bringing that fish to shore under this regulation. Those fish have been exported in uneviscerated form-guts in, if you like-for years with the support of the New Democratic Party.
We want that fish to be brought to shore so that we get first opportunity to process it, put it in its highest most value-added form; not just sockeye and pink, but chum and coho and Chinook. If they want to throw in ground-fish, I would like them to stand up and say that we want groundfish restricted to being landed at Canadian ports. I would like to hear that. I would like to know how some of their supporters who are crewmen on the trailers would feel about that. I am prepared to listen because I think it makes good sense. But I want to hear the NDP propose it in this House.

I did mention that I worked as a Member of the Cabinet to secure recognition, reinforced again last week by the Prime Minister vhile speaking in Vancouver, of the importance of the Pacific Coast salmon fishery the result of which was the conclusion of the Pacific Salmon Treaty. Members opposite have benefited by those improvements to harbours in their ridings which amount to hundreds of thousands of dollars in new multi-million dollar harbour facilities. Madam Speaker, before making my own comments I first want to express the regrets of the Member of Parliament for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Tbmer) who has for several years had a very strong concern about this issue. Unfortunately, for personal family reasons, he must be in Winnipeg today. I hope the House understands that his absence is one that he regrets. However, he had no choice but to attend to a family matter. I want to express my regrets to the House on his behalf.
In saying that, in some ways I am glad that he is not here. Having listened to 30 minutes of drivel from the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Siddon) would probably be more than any strong stomach could stand so close to the lunch hour.
Over the last two or three days many Members of Parliament have had an important experience. We have sat down and met with the workers in the West Coast fishing industry. We have talked to them about the concerns they have raised over a barbeque or over a table. What has been interesting is that people have come to the capital of the country with a simple request. They came to the Government to ask to be listened to
June 15, 1989

on a simple question. It is this. Why are they losing their jobs? Why are hard-working people who have spent years developing an effective and good industry on the West Coast, through no responsibility of their own suddenly threatened with the loss of their livelihood? It is a simple question. However, they have been unable to get answers from the Government.
We have listened to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Siddon) ramble on about all the great advantages of competitiveness and how we will make the fishing industry of Canada into a world class premium opportunity. However, he never answered the simple question as to why these people are going to lose their jobs. Why are they faced with a situation not of their own making but based upon a decision of this Government? That is the issue.
Neither the Minister nor his colleague, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), have explained why it is that it is a government decision that has put these people into this threat, that has put them into this problem. Perhaps more tragically not once have we heard from any Member on the other side what the Government is prepared to do about it. Is it really prepared to listen to these people? Is it prepared to understand the nature of the problem? From the Minister's reply today there is little hope being offered.
What is tragic is that we have a Minister of Fisheries who has the gall, the ultimate and incredible effrontery to stand up in this House and say: "The fishing industry has never had it so good". I ask him to tell the thousands of fish workers from the East Coast who have been laid off in the last month that they have never had it so good.

Right from the beginning it has taken a stand to sell out this industry with the most blatant, callous forethought.
The Government has had its public relations people working. They have churned out the press releases. The fact of the matter is it has not defended this industry.
Let me give you a little history, Madam Speaker. The great crown prince of blather, otherwise known as the Minister for International Trade, gets up to say with his hand over his heart: "The devil made me do it. It is a GATT decision. What have I to do about it?" He shrugs and sighs and moans and says: "I had no responsibility. It is the GATT that made me do it".
Madam Speaker, I will tell you what the real history is. In 1986 the Americans started complaining about this problem. At that time we were already engaged in negotiations with the Americans on the free trade deal. Things were put on the table and things were taken off. The Americans took things off the table. They said: "We are not going to talk about the Jones Act protecting the shipping industry. We are not going to talk about the Magnuson Act concerning the fish processing industry". They took those off the table. Did our Government take the West Coast fish processing industry off the table? Dam right it did not. It put it on the table. It was a bargaining chip.
When the Member from Nanaimo says that we should support the Government's strong effective stand I say that back in 1986 during that negotiation the Government had every opportunity to say to the Americans: "This is a non-negotiable item. We have the right to protect the processing of our own natural resources and we will not bargain it away". However, the Government put it on the table as part of the deal. Yet Members of the Government stand up to say that the GATT made them do it. They had two years of negotiation in which to protect the West Coast fish processing industry, and they did not take the opportunity to do it. It was there. There were certainly enough examples of things that were

However, what they do not tell Canadians, which is part of the big lie, part of the big propaganda machine that keeps going on, is that under the GATT rules it is perfectly permissible to use an export tax to protect any processing in one's own country. The GATT has allowed it with us in the past, as well as other countries. It is perfectly legitimate to use an export tax to say that raw fish leaving Canada should be subject to a higher tax.
Guess what was given away in Section 408 of the Free Trade Agreement? What was given away was the right of Canada to impose an export tax. subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today we are engaged in a discussion that is very important for the people of British Columbia. I do not rise as an expert on the fishery, but I do rise as a Member from British Columbia who is keenly aware of the importance of this industry to British Columbia and in fact to Canada, particularly to the thousands of fishermen and fish processors who are engaged in this very important livelihood.
It is essential that we focus our attention for a few moments on the history surrounding the salmon and herring fishery and that we do not forget that it was British Columbians who built the fishery, it was British Columbians who developed the product lines and the markets which make our fish products second to none in the world, and it is British Columbians who will continue to be the leaders in the trading of fish.
The concerns that have been expressed are felt by all who are close to British Columbia because the salmon and herring industry represents a major component of the B.C. economy, an economy that is dependent on trade as is the rest of the country dependent on fair and free trade. As a signatory to the GATT and to the Free Trade Agreement, Canada recognizes that there are trade rules which must be followed. We play by the rules of the game in Canada.
What is on the minds of many British Columbians is the removal of the requirements for the processing of Pacific salmon and herring in Canada. Why were these regulations removed?
In 1986 the United States indicated to Canada that it found the regulations requiring the processing of salmon and herring to be a restriction on trade. Canada and the United States entered into consultations but could not find the means to arrive at a mutually satisfactory resolution. The United States appealed as was its right to the GATT. As a result, a panel of trade experts was established to review the salmon and herring processing requirement regulations to ascertain if they constituted a GATT illegal barrier to trade.

June 15, 1989
Supply
Both Canada and the United States made their supportive arguments before the GATT panel. In November 1987 the panel ruled that in fact the processing requirements for salmon and herring could not be justified under the GATT rules and that they were a trade barrier. In April 1988 the Government accepted the GATT panel findings and indicated that the GATT illegal regulations would be removed.
This Government heard the concerns expressed by the B.C. fishing industry over the acceptance of the GATT panel findings and responded accordingly. First, it assured other sectors of the fishing industry that we were not going to take actions which would jeopardize our trading relationships around the world.
Second, it assured the fishing industry that measures would be taken to ensure that the fundamental principles of sound resource conservation and management would not be compromised by the Government's decision to accept the panel finding.
Third,it assured that any new conservation and management measures taken by the Government would be GATT consistent.
In the summer of 1988 a high level industry working group was established to identify what measures were necessary to ensure that the conservation and management of the salmon and herring industry would not be compromised by the removal of the processing requirements. It should be noted that the processing requirements constituted a de facto landing requirement and that their removal meant valuable conservation and management information could be lost.
The working group considered the problems created by the removal of the processing requirements and submitted their report in early September 1988. To ensure that any new requirements were GATT consistent, the working group recommendations were scrutinized by GATT scholars who advised the Government that some aspects of the working group's recommendations were not GATT consistent and should not be adopted by the Government.
However, the implementation of the landing requirements to ensure the collection of essential and accurate conservation and management information was considered to be GATT consistent and was implemented by this Government in April of this year. It was implemented after five lawyers gave this Government their best advice
that these new regulations were, in fact, GATT consistent.
Following the review of the working group proposals by the GATT experts, the Government undertook to discuss the new landing requirements with the United States. Bilateral discussions continued into the spring of the year with the hope that the disagreements on the landing requirements could be resolved. This has not been the case, and the matter has been referred to the free trade dispute settlement panel which will bring forward its decision in September of this year.
We have all heard the rhetoric associated with this issue, rhetoric which clouds the essential points that need to be made. I share the concerns of the B.C. workers who feel that their jobs are threatened but ask what would be the impact on the same workers if Canada was not a member of the GATT. I submit that protectionism would be the norm and B.C. and Canadian products would face trade restrictive initiatives in many of our markets.
What kind of business plan could companies or individuals prepare for a market which determines trade policy on an ad hoc basis? It would not be successful. Our membership in the GATT in recognition of the GATT rules means that we can develop products and markets with confidence. In those cases where we are treated unfairly we can appeal to the GATT for action. We should not lose sight of the importance of trade rules to effective trade and the long-term positive impact for all Canadians.
I accept, as I think we all do, the principles underlying the GATT. I accept, as I think we all should, that the Government had no other option but to abide by the GATT panel findings on Pacific salmon and herring. However, I cannot ignore the concerns of British Columbians over the potential impact of the GATT ruling. I am reassured by the action that has been taken to date, action based on sound conservation and management principles following the recommendations of the industry.
If we step away from the issue at hand and examine the B.C. fishing industry as objective observers, one cannot help but be moved by the pride this industry gives to its employees, its province, and its country. We are price setters in the market-place, not price takers, even though our products are not in the majority. When other countries have faced crisis after crisis due to inferior processing practices, our skilled and technologically
June 15, 1989

advanced industry has continued to produce top quality products.
The words "British Columbia" mean dependability and top quality around the world. Do we really need to provide trade protection for this industry? I submit that we do not. We do need to ensure that Canada's principles of conservation and management are not compromised and that no competitor is permitted to malign the B.C. reputation for quality.
The Government has initiated GATT consistent regulations to ensure that conservation and management principles are not compromised. I am confident that our fishing industry has the competitive edge and in the long term will agree that trade restrictive measures are not necessary for the continuation of this vibrant and productive industry.

BREAKDOWN OF SHARE OF PUBLIC TRANSPORT MODES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to yesterday's Globe and Mail, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) says that his Department has no detailed breakdown of the number of passengers travelling by train, bus, and airplane, and that he only has national figures from Statistics Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a. privilege for me to rise in the House today to speak about acid rain.
Thanks to the perseverance of our Government and especially of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), a major milestone was reached a few days ago, when the President of the United States presented a bill on reducing acid rain in the United States.

Canadian periodical and magazine publishers state that the cut to this postal subsidy could put them out of business. This industry only earns pre-tax profits of 2 per cent.
Studies have demonstrated the necessity of the postal subsidy for the survival of this industry. One year ago the Government announced that program funding would be maintained at approximately its current level for at least five years. That was a show and promise to Canadian voters that a Canadian cultural initiative would be preserved. With the election over, the Free Trade Agreement a fait accompli and a little pressure from American printers, the Government has broken another of its promises to Canadians.
The Government's slashing of this vital link between publisher and reader may irrevocably affect the lives of 95 per cent of Canadians who read Canadian magazines. Does this Government not realize that Canadians like to read Equinox, Chatelaine, Maclean's, and others?

subtopic: OPENING OF NEW PLANT IN TRENTON
OPENING OF NEW PLANT IN TRENTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday when I spoke in the House about the new jobs being created in my riding in the pharmaceutical industry because of good Conservative government policy, members of the Opposition complained that it was not helping their ridings at all.

It just goes to show that good government policies such as free trade are helping even those who chose not to vote Conservative, this time.

subtopic: ISSUING OF NEW RED CARD
ISSUING OF NEW RED CARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on an urgent matter. In this country we have green credit cards, gold credit cards and platinum credit cards. Now we are about to have a red card.
As the House knows, this week the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations has been conducting an investigation into the matter of credit cards. Members of this committee, from both sides of the House, have been relentless and effective in their questioning of the bankers. Some real concerns have emerged from the committee.
I wonder how the Liberal members of the committee feel about a plan that would see their Party in bed with the Royal Bank for the issuing of a new credit card. Is it right for a political Party to hand out credit cards? Is it right for a political Party to get a pay-back when a Liberal Member of Parliament uses that card for parliamentary business?
What type of signal does this send to the Liberal members of the committee who are trying to do their job in the committee? Does the Liberal Party brass not believe that this puts their members in a compromising position.

subtopic: LOW-LEVEL FLIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
LOW-LEVEL FLIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday's announcement of low-level flights in western Canada has again reminded us of a lot of what is wrong with this Government.
June 15, 1989

First, it reminds us of arrogance towards remote regions of the country when the Minister states that those areas were chosen because they are unpopulated. There is the community of La Loche in the flight path which has more than 3,000 people, and many other communities where people have lived for generations.
Secondly, there is the myth of consultation. No one along that flight path has ever been consulted. Third, the Government's thinking is still mired in the cold war. We have made it through all these years without these flights. Why do we need them now just when international relations are improving?
Therefore, I call on the Minister to get in touch with the real world and cancel these flights.

The aspect of her job that the Minister sees as uncompetitive is that she works for $14 an hour. She is protected by a union agreement with safety committees and all the supporting facilities in the plant. In addition,

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I believe you have agreed, we in the Official Opposition have agreed to divide our time into two periods of 10 and 5 versus one of 20 and 10.
I am very pleased to rise and speak on this motion today to protect the west coast of Canada jobs related to the herring and the salmon industry. This motion has to do with free trade, and it has to do with the fisheries.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY
speechtext: It has nothing to do with free trade. What bunk.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Since the passage of the Free Trade Agreement, the policy on trade is reasonably clear, if not the consequences. I wish I could say the same for the fisheries policy. If I were to ask what is the fisheries policy of Canada today, I wonder who would answer for the Government. Would it be the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) or would it be the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie)? That question is more than rhetoric because I have sat in this House and I have observed the policy questions on the fishery go back
June 15, 1989

and forth like a political tennis ball. No wonder the policy is not clear.
Today we are discussing the situation in which the Conservative Government surrendered to demands by the United States under the GATT rules for virtually unrestricted access to processed Canadian salmon and herring. These new rules, conceded on April 26 of this year, invalidated long-standing rules prohibiting the export of unprocessed salmon and herring. They require now only that fish be deposited at a designated landing station for counting prior to export. In the short term these changes threaten the loss of thousands of jobs in the processing sector in British Columbia. In the longer term they create a dangerous precedent that could signal the undermining of Canada's ability to manage and conserve valuable fisheries resources.
As if that were not enough, even this bold move was unsatisfactory to the United States Government. It threatened massive retaliation under U.S. trade laws unless Canada would guarantee that our fish could be purchased by the U.S. without it touching Canadian soil. What happened then? This Government, apparently frightened by the prospect of what Big Brother would do, offered to send even this vastly conceded issue to arbitration under the dispute mechanism of the Free Trade Agreement.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY
speechtext: It has not got to arbitration. Get your facts straight.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY
speechtext: It is going to arbitration, and the tricky part here is that the arbitrators must determine whether or not the rule changes are consistent with U.S. law, not Canadian law.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY
speechtext: My God, you are mixed up. This is absolute madness.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Not international law, but U.S. law. More and more we are being made to look like second-class citizens in our own country. That is not a very good feeling as we prepare to celebrate Canada Day with our friends and family across this country.
Now despite the many guarantees that were given on free trade during the election campaign, there is a major implication for the East Coast fishery. Now that the U.S. has successfully challenged Canadian restrictions on the
Supply
export of unprocessed fish from the West Coast, the logical next step for them would be to challenge the same type of Canadian restriction on the export of unprocessed fish from the East Coast. Whether this is because of trade policies or fisheries policies, it does not matter. Canadian fishery workers are being adversely affected by external forces, something over which this Government, any sovereign Government should have control.
I submit that just as the goal of Canada's defence policy should be to protect Canada and the interest and well-being of all Canadians, so should a fisheries policy be designed clearly and unequivocally first and foremost to protect fishermen and all those Canadians involved in the fishing industry. It is an industry that represents billions of dollars and an industry the scope and significance of which reflects Canada being the world's largest exporter of fish.
I could not believe my ears this morning when the Hon. Minister of Fisheries and Oceans suggested that we were small time on the world scale. We are the world's largest exporter of fish. No wonder we are in so much trouble. Does our present policy protect fishermen? That is the key question. I have just indicated what it will do to B.C. fishermen. What will it do to East Coast fishermen, to Newfoundland fishermen? Ask a fisherman in Bonavista Bay, Trinity Bay or Conception Bay. They wake up every morning and here is what they see. They see, first of all, signs of mismanagement. They see a giveaway of a portion of the northern cod stock in order to entice France to submit the St-Pierre and Miquelon fishing boundaries dispute to binding international arbitration just like the giveaway of processing jobs in British Columbia to the United States.
To add insult to injury, factory trawlers registered in France are harassing Newfoundlanders and their longlin-ers and they are destroying their gear in their own economic zone. They see the hope given in the 1982 Kirby Report for a total allowable catch of 400,000 tonnes reduced to a 1988 level of 255,000 tonnes. A recent recommendation by federal scientists, confirmed by a blue ribbon panel, is that the 1989 catch is going to be further reduced to 125,000 tonnes. I regret to say this, but there are signs of worse to come.

June 15, 1989
Supply
What else do these fishermen see? They see over-fishing by other foreigners, especially the Spanish and the Portuguese. In 1986, when Spain and Portugal joined the European community, the North Atlantic Fisheries Organization, NAFO, allocated 23,200 tonnes to the European community, but the community unilaterally set their own quota of 102,000 tonnes. Then they went away and took 171,000 tonnes. Similarly in 1987, NAFO gave the community 23,000 tonnes. They gave themselves
110,000	tonnes and then they took 140,000 tonnes. They give themselves five times the allocation and then go off to catch seven times the allocation.
Stemming from this mismanagement, with the acknowledgement of the serious depletion of northern cod stocks, they see the possibility of an ecological disaster, one that will not only wreck the economy of Newfoundland but one that will savage communities in Nova Scotia and will affect seriously the coastal communities of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
Furthermore, with the announcement of the Government to retire the venerable tracker fleet as part of the CFB Summerside shutdown, they see a cut-back in surveillance and control so crucial to police these waters and the 250 floating trawler fish plants in our own inshore and offshore economic zone. These aircraft provide 800 of the 900 flying hours of fisheries surveillance in the Atlantic. Given the mismanagement and the ecological catastrophe issues that we are facing, there should be at least a reasonable expectation of the opposite.
They see the loss of jobs despite what has been said here. There are 65,000 registered fishermen in Atlantic Canada and 30,000 plant workers in 900 plants.
There are 14,000 people employed in the B.C. fish harvesting and processing industry. These jobs, as we see here today, are being seriously jeopardized.
There is something else that we see. We see band-aid regulations and policies, perhaps well intentioned, but these policies confuse and anger our fishermen. I want to give you one example, Madam Speaker.
We have in Newfoundland a new crab closure policy for the Newfoundland region which came into effect on January 31 this year. In all fairness to the Department and its officials, the objective of this new policy was to
ensure uniformity of closures throughout all districts and to reduce the risk of quota overruns. The new policy stated that at midnight on the pre-announced closure date, no crab would be permitted to be landed. That is to say that if there was any crab found in the crab pots, they had to be left in the ocean. They could not be retained.
The key to making this procedure work was that ample warning time be given to the fishermen. Ample time depends on a number of things, such as the number of traps set, the size of the vessel and weather conditions, all individually variable and variable as a combination. What might be acceptable to a 65-footer with 800 traps over a calm period would clearly not be ample for a 40-footer in rough weather with a different number of traps.
The end result in Bonavista Bay last week was that the time given was such that when the quota was reached and the closure was announced, many fishermen did not have sufficient time to clear their pots and return then-catch for processing ashore. They had to dump them instead. We have a situation in which the crab were caught but the fishermen had to get up in the middle of the night, steam out, haul their pots, return the crab to the ocean and come back without their catch. They were angiy and upset. I think they had every reason to be so. Under the conditions and with the new policy in force more warning time was needed.
Are these policies protecting our fishermen? They do not think so. Quite frankly, I do not think so. I am sure that there are Members in the House on this side and opposite who do not think so either. These fishermen are honest, hard-working and trusting people. I believe they have been let down by the Government. They would certainly not agree with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans that they never had it so good.
I could go on relating these ills from now until the House shuts down on June 30, if it closes down then. Fishermen have to cope with an awful lot. However, I do not want to look backward. Life is interesting looking backward but, unfortunately, it has to be lived forward.
What we need is an overhaul of our fisheries policy that will offer protection for fishermen. Plainly and simply, we need a fisheries policy that will guarantee jobs for our fishermen and our plant workers. We need to raise the profile of the fishing industry so that it becomes an issue of national importance and concern. Finally, we need accompanying and foreign policies that will imple-
June 15, 1989

ment and support our fisheries policies, ones that will make our industry healthy, viable and vibrant.
As a Member hailing from a riding so predominantly dependent on the fishery, I strongly support this motion that this House reaffirms the Government's pledge to the West Coast salmon and herring industry not to allow jobs historically established to be threatened by any government response to GATT rulings.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
I thought that this was a debate about the West Coast salmon and herring industry. The hon. gentleman opposite spent all his time talking about the fishery on the East Coast. These two fisheries are some
3,000	miles apart. If the hon. gentleman knows as much about the West Coast fishery as he knows about the East Coast fishery, God help us.
When I get to my own remarks I will expand on this issue. The dispute about the salmon and herring regulations on the West Coast of Canada has absolutely nothing to do with the Free Trade Agreement. It was a complaint initiated in 1986. It was a complaint brought under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, not brought under American legislation or under the Free Trade Agreement, which did not then exist.
This is a dispute about what the GATT international trading rules mean or do not mean in relation to certain regulations. When this matter goes, by the way, to a panel under the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, the panel is not going to consider American law at all. American law does not come into the matter. It will not be considered.
What the panel will be considering is Chapter 18. It will examine the consistency of Canada's landing requirements for Pacific salmon and herring with our obligations under the GATT. That is what it will be examining.
The hon. gentleman referred to the protection of fishermen. I will be able to elaborate on this in my own remarks. I want to point out to him that if Canada ignores the results of the GATT panel with reference to these regulations on the West Coast of Canada, the United States would be justified under the GATT in taking retaliatory action against Canada. Whatever the amount of the trade damage was that it had suffered as a
Supply
result of our continuing with regulations that were GATT inconsistent and damaging it, it could take counter measures against Canadian exports to the United States. The Americans could choose whatever Canadian exports they like to take those counter retaliatory measures against. They might well choose to counter retaliate against East Coast fishery products-lobster from the East Coast, or cod, or whatever. I would like to hear what the hon. gentleman would be saying about the situation because Canada ignored a GATT panel decision, and his own fishermen on the East Coast were injured as a result. I would like to hear what the hon. gentleman would then say about that particular situation.

I have to remind him that I grew up in a family that had been in the fishing business for seven generations. I am sure the Minister would agree that some of this has to rub off on one at some time.

We are adding insult to injury. It is no wonder that these people are upset. I say once more, I more strongly support this motion the more I hear from Members opposite.

Madam Speaker, I say to my friend from St. John's West, we will see whether it is repetition or not. I will let him

June 15, 1989

decide. He has the opportunity to follow me, I would think. I look forward to hearing what he has to say.
First, I want to congratulate the hon. gentleman from Nanaimo-Cowichan for bringing this motion forward, and for putting it down in such eloquent terms. For the eloquence he cannot take all the credit, I say to him. The eloquence actually belongs to another Member of this Chamber. We ought to give credit where it is due. The eloquence is that of the gentleman who happens right now to be the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Siddon). The words are largely his. It was he who said first that the Government would "not allow jobs, historically established, to be threatened" by government actions.
Those were his words, Madam Speaker. I congratulate my friend for Nanaimo-Cowichan for putting down this resolution in words which are clearly going to be acceptable, certainly to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon). If there ever was a motherhood resolution, this has to be it. It calls upon the House to reaffirm the Government's pledge not to allow the salmon and herring industry to be threatened by any Government response to GATT rulings. I would expect that the entire Government would want to support that particular resolution. I do.
I would like to state in the next few minutes why I do. I have had some visits, as I am sure many Members have had in the past few days, from people who have come all the way from Prince Rupert and from other parts of British Columbia to acquaint us with some of the details of the situation which they face. I represent a fishing constituency which I believe is the largest one in the country in terms of numbers of persons who depend on employment in the fishery, either in catching the resource or processing the resource. There are 16,000 such persons in Burin-St. George's. I claim to represent the largest fishing riding in all of Canada.
I found common cause when I heard those people from Prince Rupert and other parts of British Columbia, and when I saw the thoroughness with which they had prepared their case. I believe many Members of the House will be familiar with this particular document, an appeal to Canadians, which I hold here. Also for the edification of the gentleman who is the Minister of Fisheries, I will quote some more of his words. On November 17, 1987, he said that: "I give you my assurance that those jobs are safe." Of course, he was talking about the jobs in B.C. which are very much the subject of
this motion today. "I give you my assurance that those jobs are safe." That was November 17, 1987.
By May 3, 1989, a month or so ago, he was saying something quite different: "I have never said the specific jobs would remain intact." I submit that these are two completely mutually exclusive statements. He either means one or the other. He cannot mean both unless the gears are changed along the way. Clearly, that is what has happened in this particular case. The people who prepared this brochure are quite justified in labelling that part of their brochure the betrayal of an industry.
Had I the time, Madam Speaker, I could talk to you at some length about the betrayal of the fishing industry on the East Coast. However, today, let us stay for a moment with the West Coast. Before we do, let us go to a gentleman from South Shore in whose riding is located the fish plant at Lockeport. He has said quite recently, less than a month ago, on May 16 that: "We are exporting 1,000 jobs a year from Nova Scotia along with our roundfish". That was from a Member in the same Party as the Minister of Fisheries, who lauded his Government today and the administration which he is part of, for how it was getting the best dollar, in his words, how he was seeing to it single-handedly that we were encouraging further processing. I have to say to him, that is not at all what the figures say.
I have this fresh from Statistics Canada just a few minutes ago and it states that in 1988, our primary export in the fishery-that is to say whole, dressed, fillets and blocks-last year for all of Canada 371.9 thousand metric tons. That is the figure to keep in mind. If we compare that to the exports we did in the fishing industry after secondary processing had been affected, that is, smoked, cured, salted, canned and so on, the figure is 204.9 thousand metric tons, or a ratio of approximately two to one. We are still exporting essentially in the unprocessed form two-thirds of all the fish we catch in this country.
Why the Minister of Fisheries can stand there and brag about that escapes me completely. He said something else that needs just a quick rebuttal. He said, and I copied his words down this morning: "Canada is near the top as a competitive nation." He said we are way down from No. 11 and now near the top. I agree with him on one thing. We are way down. I will tell him how far down now. I have this from the World Bank in its latest economic atlas, which compares growth rates for the 1980 to 1987 period. The World Bank states that Canada does not stand first or second, as the Minister is saying, and as the Minister for Consumer and Corporate Affairs
June 15, 1989

(Mr. Valcourt) has been saying recently. It does not stand first and second at all.
Here is what the World Bank says. That is the organization that my good friend from St. John's West is going to- I want to be the first to predict this publicly- when he leaves here, which is sooner than a lot of people think. He has got his mind essentially made up, he is going to the World Bank. I believe that he will be the new president of the World Bank. He will then have to espouse those very figures. I say to him today: "Tread softly. Don't do anything and don't say anything which might turn off your prospective employers a year or two down the road." The World Bank stated that: Canada is not in the first or second in terms of growth. In the last eight years, it actually stands forty-sixth. Forty-five countries have managed to grow faster than Canada in the past seven or eight years.

Nor is Canada at the top of the league among the industrialized countries. speechtext:
The GATT panel made its finding. We considered the matter and negotiated with the United States for a number of months. On March 22, 1988 we announced our intention to remove the GATT inconsistent measures and to replace them with measures that would be GATT consistent. That is what we have done. We have had a series of consultations with the industry, with the union and with the British Columbia Government. We have had meeting after meeting in devising a new set of landing regulations that will act to help in the proper management and conservation of the B.C. salmon and herring stocks.
The main purpose of these regulations is to better manage the B.C. salmon stocks and to ensure conservation. No one can sell over the side. Everyone is required to land as of late in April when the new regulations were passed. You have to land your fish at an approved landing station. The fish had to go through, be observed, measured, and certain biological tests and checks had to be done so that we have the proper information to
Supply
manage and conserve the B.C. salmon stocks. After that has happened, anyone who wants to buy the salmon can buy it.
By the way, one has to assume it is a bit better for the B.C. fishermen. The more competition there is to buy their fish the better it is for them. One has to assume that the Alaskan fishermen are not complaining because Canadian buyers can buy Alaska salmon or that Canadians can buy Alaska herring. The more competition for the fish the better the price. But here are these great NDPers over here, how they love the fishermen, how they want to protect the fishermen. They do not even see any conflict of interest in what they are doing and saying here. There is a conflict of interest between the interests of the fishermen and the interests of the fish processing workers which the New Democrats do not even pretend to notice.
During 1988, we had consultation between the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the B.C. industry union and the provincial government. Then on March 29, the U.S. trade representative told us that even our new proposed regulations are considered to be unfair trading practices. So on April 25, we revoked the old regulations because they are clearly trade restrictive and inconsistent with the GATT. We put in place the new landing requirements for Pacific salmon and herring.
We believe that given a chance, this system will help ensure good management and quality of B.C. salmon. Incidentally, it will also be helpful to those who are worried about the B.C. processing industry.
We are getting no help from the NDP Members. None whatsoever. They are not giving us any ammunition to support these new landing regulations. No. They are giving all the ammunition to the United States people who are going to appear before the GATT panel. They are going to have all the protectionist statements of the NDP Members from British Columbia to use as evidence before the panel. They do not care if they help the Americans. All they care about is trying to score a few cheap political points in this House. They do not care about the good of the fish processing workers. They do not care about the fishermen. They do not care about anything but trying to skulldug themselves into power.

On May 23, 1989, the U.S. requested a dispute settlement panel be established under Chapter 18 of the Free Trade Agreement. That panel is going to examine the consistency of these landing requirements with our obligations under the GATT. That is the question. We are lucky enough to have three Canadian members on that panel. We have two Canadian nominees to the panel and two Americans nominees. They could not agree on a chairman. They had to choose a chairman by lot. The chairman is going to be another Canadian, the dean of the law school here in Ottawa who formerly taught out at UBC, I believe, the University of British Columbia. So we have a Canadian chairman on this panel, two Canadian members and two American members. They will do their job in accordance with international trade rules and they will examine the system to see whether they feel this system is GATT-consistent or not. If we happen to lose that case, the blame will fall squarely upon Members of the New Democratic Party in this House.
Canadians have not lost their right to access fish caught in their own waters. They are the only ones who can catch fish in their own waters. It is our administration and our rules that say there are no over-the-side sales. The fishermen of British Columbia are to catch the salmon and herring.
The representatives from British Columbia do not care about the position of the fishermen. They think they are onto some other political point that is going to do better for them than the cause of the fishermen and fish processing workers. But we are protecting both. We are protecting the B.C. fishermen who are going to have the sole right to catch the fish in B.C. and Canadian waters and we are protecting the fish processing workers, because these regulations are going to assist the management and conservation of the industry. I think they are going to continue, the result of which will be that I will be surprised if not all the fish caught in B.C. waters, but nearly all, do not continue to be processed there.

speechtext: You would be surprised? Is that all you are prepared to do is be surprised?
