The Hon. Member will not be surprised because he is in the House telling untruths. He is in here pretending people have lost their jobs when they have not lost their jobs. He is trying to scare the wits out of people unnecessarily. He does not want to be helpful.
There have been months of work done on this. There are resources committed to the west coast salmon industry which doubtless the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) has expanded on what has been spent through the Salmonid Enhancement Program and other programs. I notice from my notes here that it is $41 million a year.
The GATT is the cornerstone of Canadian trade policy. It served us well over the years. We sometimes win at the GATT and we sometimes lose at the GATT. But if we, as one of the medium-sized powers of the world, are going to abandon the GATT when it does not suit our own narrow interests and not accept our obligations as a trading partner in the system, then the system is doomed and Canada is doomed because Canada depends on trade for our prosperity. One-third of our whole national wealth comes from that trade. Four million Canadians depend on exports. Members opposite want to jeopardize four million Canadians while they try to scare a couple of thousand other Canadians. This is the kind of statesmanship we get from the New Democratic Party, Madam Speaker.
We depend on strong and predictable international trade rules to protect our own export sales. A strong GATT is the best security we have for Canadian trade. How can we turn our back on it? There are individual cases where we do not particularly like the results but we have had to recognize certain regulations were not GATT-consistent.
By the way, the situation on the East Coast is that regulations that were in place are grandfathered under the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. That has nothing to do with this situation. However, anyone who wants to challenge even the east coast regulations under the GATT could do so. There is nothing to prevent that from happening. It simply cannot be challenged under the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement. The United States would not agree, because of their success in this case, of grandfathering the B.C. regulations under the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement. They would still have been exposed to a challenge under the GATT in any event as they were challenged in 1986.
Let us forget all the rhetoric and forget the attempts to confuse the issue.
June 15, 1989

I might point to Mr. Peter Pearse's report. He ran for the Liberal Party in the last election. In his report of 1982, he said this:
Although pressure from established processors and plant workers to restrict exports of less highly processed products is understandable, to do so is inconsistent with fishermen's interest in high prices and with the public interest in generating the highest returns from resources.
Of course, Hon. Members opposite are not interested in the fishermen's interest in high prices. We already know that.
Just to reiterate, no jobs have been lost. None. No jobs. We have a new set of regulations in place that we think will protect Canada's and British Columbia's interests, the interests of the industry and the people in the industry out there. Canadian fishermen are not going to be damaged in any event. Only Canadian fishermen can catch the salmon and herring. We have an increase in plant workers and fishermen in the last four years as the result of our efforts and policies. These are the facts.
We have worked hard to put the system in place that we have now. We need the support of the Members from British Columbia, the industry, and the unions of British Columbia to maintain our position in the panel that is now going to operate under the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement. What we need is help, not hindrance by Members of the New Democratic Party.

Here would be the situation if we did what the hon. gentleman is suggesting we do. The United States or some country goes to GATT. GATT establishes a panel. The panel finds that Canada's particular regulations are inconsistent with GATT and with the world international trading rules which have been in effect since 1947. Canada accepts the GATT panel report as it must and should do, if we believe in a world trading system in which we are so totally dependent, and then we turn around and add an export tax and vitiate the whole results of the GATT panel report.
Does the Hon. Member think the other countries of the world in the GATT trading system will put up with that, or that this would be consistent with GATT? You win on the one side, and then the country against which you are successful comes in and imposes an export tax.
At the present time an export tax might well be permitted under the terms of the GATT. However, with respect to the United States of America under the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement, we have both agreed not to impose export taxes on goods that we sell to one another which are consumed in the country to which we sell them.
If we sell the Americans goods that they are to consume themselves in the United States, we are prevented from imposing an export tax. In the same manner, the United States is prevented from imposing an export tax on goods that we import from them to consume in Canada.
Why is that? Because it is a free trade agreement. We are going to reduce tariffs between our two countries over 10 years, so there are no longer any tariffs. If there are to be no longer any tariffs, how can we have export taxes and put on the reverse of tariffs so in effect there is a tariff going in the other direction? Part of a free trade

agreement is that two countries agree not to put export taxes on the goods that one another consumes.
However, if the United States wanted to import something from Canada to re-export somewhere else and not to consume in the United States, then an export tax would be valid with respect to those goods.
I hope that clarifies the matter for the hon. gentleman, although I think his mind being so murky it would take a lot more than my abilities to clear anything up for him.

Surely, it will not be against the fishermen and the plant workers on the East Coast or the West Coast. They have already suffered that pain. speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
We can talk about who said this and that. We can talk about who should have done this and that, but this is not a roll of the dice. This is the responsibility of a Government that swore on behalf of the people that they were going to protect the jobs of those workers. I say they put them at risk and they say they have not. If I am wrong, I am prepared to walk away from it by saying that I put my seat on it. They should be prepared to do the same.
Let the Minister of Fisheries stand up in this House today and say, as it is in this resolution, that not a job will be lost, and that if a job is lost, I will step down from my seat. Let the Minister of International Trade with all of his bluster and nonsense and personal attacks say that if I am wrong, I too will step down because I put too much at stake on the roll of the dice. Let me predict this. Should this happen in British Columbia, God help us, it is going to happen in the Atlantic provinces as sure as the sun comes up in the morning because Americans will see how weak-kneed, how stupid and how lacking in ability this Government is in dealing with these kinds of issues. We are not going to score debating points about you said this and I said that. That is all nonsense now. Now the crunch has come.
In a few weeks the fishing season will start. Yes, the British Columbia fishermen will catch the fish as they have always done and as they have always had a right to do. To pronounce in this House that somehow the Government has protected this inherent right by Canada being a sovereign nation is nonsense. The fishermen will catch the fish. Who will process the fish is the question? We predict that once those fish are in this phoney landing situation, they will be scooped up by American

buyers, trucked down to American plants and off to Japan.
What the Minister said in his last hidden comment in response to an answer of my colleague was about the export taxes. We cannot put an export tax on anything consumed in the United States. Ninety-five per cent of the canning of Canadian fish under this agreement will not be consumed in the United States. It will be sold offshore for a massive profit by the American processors. If the Americans had to eat all the fish that they imported from Canada, they would have fish three times a day and an extra meal at midnight trying to get through those cans. Who is he trying to kid? It is not for consumption in the United States. It is for the export market, trans-shipped and processed through the United States. You have sold us out. You have sold out British Columbia. You have sold out the people of my province and you play games in here.
Thank you, Madam Speaker. I know my time is up. I repeat calmly and rationally that if I am wrong, I will resign my seat. I expect from either one of those Ministers to respond to my challenge by saying that if they are wrong, they will resign their seat.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to touch on a few of the things that have been raised by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Siddon) and the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) today. There is a very fundamental issue that has to be addressed in this debate. It is that one cannot compete if one does not have the fish.
What we are talking about here is the ideological and the philosophical approach that we just heard once again from the Hon. Member from Halifax. He said: "Go talk to the fishermen". He thinks that is the solution.
Let me run through a few of the designs that we see coming out of the ideology of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, or as Alan Fotheringham refers to it, the regressive convertibles.
What is going on in the high seas? We know that Japan, Taiwan, Singapore and Korea are involved in a massive drift-net fishery-50,000 miles of drift-nets this year. They are taking between one-fifth and one-third of
British Columbian salmon. What does the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans do? He wrings his hands. He will send five observers out to go on 1,500 boats. He is a real tough guy. He is really out there standing up for Canada. He is a great Canadian.
What does the same Minister of Fisheries do for Alcan? Alcan wants to take all the water out of a river system in British Columbia. It is dealt with in Section 20(10) of the Fisheries Act, one of the oldest constitutional and parliamentary powers in Canada in relation to flowing water and fish. What does he do? He signs on the dotted line. He gives up all powers and turns over those spawning areas in those river systems to the Aluminum Company of Canada so that they can make power to export where? To the United States.
What did he do on the Queen Charlotte Islands when Frank Bevan Logging caused a big slide? The slide went down into the river system and blocked the salmon four seasons in a row so that they cannot get in. We win every way. We win in provincial court. We win in the Court of Appeal. We win in the Supreme Court of British Columbia. The case is on its way to the Supreme Court of Canada so that we can get the logging companies to pay restitution for cleaning out the stream. In the middle of the election what does the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans do? He drops the charges.
There is a design here on the high seas and in the rivers. What about pollution? Some 17 out of the 23 pulp mills in British Columbia have been in significant noncompliance with their permits for more than a year, accounting for 50 per cent of the marine pollution in Canada. We will have fisheries closed right in Prince Rupert. Fishermen cannot even take crab, prawn or shrimp out of the harbour because they are polluted with dioxin. What does the Minister of Fisheries do? He sits on a 600-page report that demonstrates that almost every pulp mill in Canada is in significant non-compliance with the Fisheries Act of Canada. Does he do anything? He does diddly-squat. There are only two places in this country where wool grows. One is on the back of a sheep and the other is inside the skulls of the Minister for International Trade and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. That is clear to anyone who studies this issue for even a moment.
June 15, 1989

Let us go back to where this all began. Let us go back to the grand design. What did the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans say in Prince Rupert? Let me quote his words. We used to have CBC in Prince Rupert but the Toiy ideology was that regions of the country cannot have news and weather. No, we have to get rid of the CBC. Here is what the Minister of Fisheries had to say in Prince Rupert on CBC. I quote: "If we are talking about liberalizing trade, and we are talking about free trade talks, maybe we should be talking about the free flow of fish between the two countries," referring to Canada and the United States.
When the former U.S. Ambassador to Canada, Thomas Niles, was asked out in British Columbia about what some of the articles of the Free Trade Agreement meant when it came to logging he said that his understanding of the Free Trade Agreement was that it would mean that U.S. loggers would be able to come into British Columbia, fell trees, buck trees, load the trees and take those trees back to the United States. I am paraphrasing what he said. However, it is on the public record.
We hear a lot of buffalo chips from the Minister for International Trade. He says: "This will not affect Maritime Canada, the East Coast, Newfoundland, P.E.I., Nova Scotia".
The same GATT challenge to which the Government acquiesced supinely out in British Columbia is going to affect New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Quebec. I urge people in those provinces to read Article 1205.
It is the same ideology, the same philosophy. This whole process to sell out the fishing industry all over Canada began on April Fools Day, 1986. The decision had been made in Cabinet. They never told the backbenchers. I do not suspect for a moment that most Tory Members of Parliament know what the underlying agreements are between Canada and the U.S. on this.
I know all of the issues that brought Icicle Seafoods about. We could not buy and bring those fish into Prince Rupert if they were not surplus to the plants in the State of Alaska. The Ministers never want to talk about that. The Ministers do not want to talk about the Magnuson Act. They act as though it did not exist. We cannot do in
Supply
U.S. waters what they claim to want to be able to do in ours.
What happened, Madam Speaker? My colleague for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca (Mr. Barrett) made it very clear. The actual applicants from Icicle made it very clear. The maximum damage they tried to seek under 301 was $5 million. What does this Government do? It puts an $867 million industry from last year on the ropes, on the chance. There is no certainty that Icicle could have even won it. But the Government put our entire industry on the block for $5 million. It does not even want to fight it.
Then what happened? We get this GATT panel in Geneva. It is unbelievable. Someone was sent who knew almost nothing about law. He stood up for Canada, at the very best on his knees. He did not argue on the principles of the Law of the Sea, the covenants of the International Law of the Sea which gives us very specific identifiable rights, which predate the Magnuson Act of 1976. Was that argued? No. This was by design all the way along. This was a coldly, calculated way of fudging the issue all the way along.
Let me give another issue of fudging, Madam Speaker, from the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon). What did he say while this matter was in Geneva? I asked the question right here on the floor of the House. He said right here in this House of Commons and I quote: "What we have here is a panel recommendation which will in all likelihood be overturned by the GATT Council". We, speaking for the Government of Canada on the floor of the House of Commons, said we will be opposing the recommendation when it reaches the GATT Council. That is what he said. Shore workers and fishermen in British Columbia said that the Government blew it in terms of allowing it to get where it has got. It gets to the GATT panel. We do not even argue on Canada's behalf, do not argue for Canada's outstanding position which we would have won. We allow it to be lost there. We then say we are going to oppose it when it goes to GATT Council. Does Canada oppose it? Fat chance. On March 21,1988, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) capitulated to U.S. interests.

June 15, 1989

On March 22, 1988, what happened? Well, history speaks for itself. What went on in Washington? The fishermen were told: "Okay, don't worry, we are going to have a working group in terms of getting some new regulations." Bear in mind, these regulations date from 1903 in terms of herring and salmon in British Columbia. It massively predates the FTA, and predates GATT by more than 40 years.
There are principles of international law which must be upheld if the international forum is to survive. The Minister states that we have to be GATT-consistent and a lot of other bluster and bull. History is very clear about what happened here. This was a sell-out by design.
Who do we send to Washington after we had been promised in the working group, we were promised landing rights? We were promised grading rights and we were promised evisceration. We were told Canadians have a right to gut fish. If we do not have a right to gut fish, logs will go to the United States. Do we ship pigs? Do we shoot hogs in this country and ship them with their guts into the United States? Do we do it to chickens or anything else? This is the thin edge of the wedge.
If you will just give me a moment, Madam Speaker, I will close on a couple of quick points. What went on in Washington is crucial. We sent down how Howie Wilson. Who did the United States have on their side? They had Peter Murphy who had just been through the whole FTA negotiation with Simon Reisman. He knew exactly how deep the desire to sell out the fishing industry was from the Conservative Government. It was a chip, a bargaining pawn in relation to other agenda items. Madam Speaker, earlier this afternoon we heard from the Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby). I think fisher people around British Columbia and around this land will have listened with care when he said: "Talk to the fishermen. You have a right to catch fish but that is as far as it goes". After that, it is free enterprise, he would have liked to have said.
Let me deal with what my hon. colleague for Nickel Belt has just raised. It is abundantly clear what the implications are in terms of the thin edge of the wedge. We can see it directly and visibly in Articles 1203, 1204 and 1205, as to how the fishing industry in other areas of the country will be challenged on precisely the same grounds as what happened in British Columbia.
In terms of any kind of prohibitory provincial or federal law, such as that to have to process nickel in a certain area of Ontario, as an example. It will simply be a

matter of time before the argument espoused by the Member from Halifax is used in that situation.
They will say that once the nickel is mined then it is up to the open market. That means situations where we have in fact become, as we are in the B.C. fishing industry, the most competitive, the world leader in terms of price and quality. We have done that over generations. We are doing it in other sectors in our economy. However, let us not forget what Thomas Niles had to say when he spoke about our forest industry, because he had been briefed about what the FTA really means.
According to him, even though the export of logs of all species is in Article 1203, the same place where we find the. fish regulations, his interpretation is that U.S. citizens, under U.S. law, will be able to come into Canada and cut our trees down and take them back to the mills in their country.
If this debate does not alert Canadians to the underlying ideology and the ultimate goal of what was negotiated between our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and President Reagan, and if people cannot see it now in relation to what is going on in the fishing industry, they then will not understand why Members of Parliament like myself will be standing on the docks and doing whatever is necessary, including civil disobedience, to make sure that our fish are not exported, regardless of the smelly deals cut by the Conservative Party of Canada to sell out our nation.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-WEST COAST SALMON AND HERRING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to stand in the House today and speak on this very important matter to British Columbians. As a native British Columbian and one who has spent a great deal of time on the north coast, as well as the west coast of Vancouver Island, I realize the importance of this topic to all of us in British Columbia and indeed across Canada. One of the things we have not talked about too much in the debate this afternoon is whether or not Canadians can compete in this world, and that is what I would like to talk about this afternoon.
It has been asked what the Government will do to help the West Coast industry in the face of the current
Supply
salmon and herring situation. One should not be left with the impression that the West Coast is being abandoned. The West Coast fishery, like most other world fisheries, has gone through and will continue to go through both turbulent times and prosperous times. Since 1985, the industry has been both buoyant and prosperous.
The Pacific fishery is dominated by salmon which in 1987 accounted for approximately 46 per cent of the total landed value of $416 million. Herring, mainly roe herring, accounted for 26 per cent of it and groundfish for 22 per cent, with shellfish and the remainder types making up the balance of landings.
Can West Coast fishermen remain competitive? To respond to this question one must realize the tremendous pressures on West Coast fish stocks. To take salmon as an example, apart from ocean survival and environmental concerns, these fish must first pass through U.S. and Canadian commercial fisheries as well as recreational and native fisheries before returning to their streams of origin. Within these returning stocks, there are weak and strong runs of fish, enhanced and wild stocks of all five species of salmon. To ensure that adequate escapement takes place makes the business of fisheries management extremely complex and fisheries managers must exercise extreme caution. All fishing plans in British Columbia are designed to target specifically those stocks which are expected to be returning in abundance and to minimize or avoid the harvest of weaker stocks which cannot withstand commercial harvest.
In 1976, in response to declines in many salmon stocks, the federal Government launched the Salmonid Enhancement Program, SEP, which to date has invested one quarter of a billion dollars to rebuild depleted salmon stocks and enhance fishing opportunities. SEP continues a formal commitment by the federal Government and the Province of B.C. to an extensive systematic program of enhancement of salmonid stocks.
In 1987, 607 million juvenile salmon and sea-run trout were released from enhancement projects. The resulting catch in escapement through 1991 is anticipated to be
8,570,000	fish plus. In 1985, enhancement contributed approximately 14 per cent by weight and 21 per cent by landed value to the commercial salmon fishery catch.

June 15, 1989
Supply
By the early 1990s, SEP is expected to account for one third of British Columbia's salmonid production. SEP has been the vehicle allowing approximately 12,000 volunteers to help enhance and rebuild the resource and has served to increase the public's awareness of the importance of protecting fish habitat. By 1990-91, the funding commitment to SEP will stabilize at $42.5 million a year and 19 of SEP's projects are contracted out to remote native communities in B.C., thus providing training and experience for natives as well as economic development opportunities.
SEP is an increasing factor in B.C. fisheries. It is a program aimed at ensuring that future prospects for this valuable resource will be greatly improved. Maintenance of a program such as SEP clearly indicates the Government's commitment to fostering a strong West Coast fisheries resource base.
Prior to 1985, the SEP program could not expand to realize its full potential because many stocks targeted for enhancement were being fished in Alaska and Washington. As a result, following almost two decades of negotiations, the Pacific Salmon Treaty was signed in March of 1985. This treaty sets out long-term goals for the benefit of salmon. The principles of the treaty are to prevent overfishing and to provide for optimum protection and for each party to receive benefits equivalent to the production of salmon originating in its waters.
Why did we need the Pacific Salmon Treaty? Salmon fishery managers in Canada and the United States are challenged by the fact that some of the Pacific salmon each country produces are intercepted by fishermen of the other country. Interception exists because salmon swim across international borders beyond the jurisdiction of the Government in whose waters they were spawned. The fish migrate long distances, spending several years at sea. In the course of their migratory cycle, United States spawned fish enter the fishery zones of Canada and Canadian fish enter U.S. waters where they are vulnerable to the other country's fishing fleets.
Over the years, research by both countries revealed that Alaskan fishermen were catching salmon bound for British Columbia, Oregon and Washington. Canadian fishermen were capturing Coho, Chinook and other species bound for the rivers of Washington and Oregon. Fishermen in northern British Columbia were intercepting salmon returning to Alaska, and United States fishermen were catching salmon as they travelled
through the Strait of Juan de Fuca and San Juan Islands toward Canada's Fraser River.
Unless management policies and conservation concerns are jointly agreed on, one nation may harvest too many of the other country's stocks and frustrate the home country's management plans. Uncontrolled interceptions may also jeopardize the administrative and financial support needed for salmon enhancement programs. The home country may be reluctant to invest in hatcheries for habitat protection and restoration if the fish produced are caught by fishermen of another nation. Intercepting fisheries encourage over-harvest and discourage investment in conservation and enhancement.
Through the years, the United States and Canada reached agreements over the management of particular salmon stocks in limited regions, for example Fraser River Sockeye and pink salmon. However, the number and diversity of each country's intercepting fisheries defied small-scale solutions. The Pacific Salmon Treaty is broad in scope, enabling it to serve as the means to co-ordinated management of the coast-wide salmon resource.
Management of the West Coast fishery is not a simple task. The Department, for example, has the following objectives for the salmon fishery: First, it wants to achieve escapement objectives by ensuring that each salmon stock or groups of stocks are not overfished. It wants to ensure that the international obligations for all five species of salmon under the new Pacific Salmon Treaty are met and it wants to ensure that the domestic allocation of the total allowable catch between sectors, whether native, commercial or recreational, and within sectors, whether seiners, gill netters or trailers, are achieved.
Verification programs are necessary to confirm which species are caught, where they are caught as well as what stocks make up the catch. As each fishery commences, Department of Fisheries officers collect catch and biological information on the harvested species. The first stage, hailing, provides information to DFO on the fishing grounds by fishermen. This information is subsequently verified at the second stage when the catch is delivered to landing stations and reported to the Depart-
June 15, 1989

ment on sales slips. Estimates of catch and catch rates are calculated and fishing plans are adjusted accordingly.
Some biological information is gathered on the grounds but the bulk of sampling, and I think this is key to the topic we are talking about today, is done as the harvested salmon are being delivered to shore-based landing stations, hence the need for a landing requirement. Catch and biological sampling programs which verify what has been caught by species and stock are the key elements of a salmon conservation program.
To meet national and international obligations and to protect the resource from overfishing, fish managers must gather and verify this information quickly and adjust harvest plans accordingly. The integrity of these programs must be maintained to optimize production of salmon in B.C., and this is the reason we are insisting upon the landing regulations that are the topic of the debate today.
Careful husbandry of the fisheries resource has allowed the stocks in most West Coast fisheries to remain abundant. The West Coast fishery has seen days of depleted stocks, such as herring.
In the early 1970s the whole fishery had to be shut down. However, recognition by the industry as a whole- this includes the Government, fishermen and the shore workers-of the problem and subsequent good management practices by the Government have allowed these stocks to rebuild to allow solid fishing opportunities and the maintenance of strong markets.
The management techniques practised by Canada are further extended by a committed inspection service that allows Canadian products to maintain a top position in world markets. We are concerned about the quality our Canadian products are presenting to the world, and it is important in the whole competitive arena.
I asked if West Coast fishermen and shore workers can remain competitive. I say absolutely. As you have heard, Madam Speaker, various programs are in place, of which I have only given a sample, to ensure that fishermen have healthy stocks of fish to harvest. They have been ridiculing the depletion of stocks on the East Coast, yet when the same thing is done on the West Coast it becomes a bad thing. This is the whole concept of
Supply
fisheries management. Stocks are allocated and, for commercial fishermen, landed to be sold.
Can the industry as a whole remain competitive? Absolutely. With a strong competitive market, fishermen will surely be able to demand top price for top quality fish as they currently do. Processors with labels that are synonymous with premium quality fish should surely want to purchase top quality fish and maintain their niche in the market. To process the fish, workers will be needed in the plants.
Can Canadian fish companies remain competitive? I say they can. The Government has invested heavily in the development and management of Canadian fisheries. Our management practices and fish inspection services are respected in today's international fishing forums. We may need to make changes in how we do business to adjust to changing times. But the basic premise of Canada maintaining strong viable fisheries for the benefit of all Canadians will always remain. Yes, we are now facing a dispute with our friends to the south but it will be resolved. The combination of government management of the resource and private enterprise initiative to process and market the resource, will prevail. Canada can be competitive in today's market and in the climate of free trade.

Madam Speaker, I wonder if the Hon. Member would care to comment on the correspondence between the State of Washington from Skagit County and processors in British Columbia. One letter in particular, from Mr. Don Miller, President of Great Northern Packing, pointed out all of the various benefits that there would be for the processing industry from B.C. to move there. Under the tax credit section of the proposal to get the processing industry to move to Washington it states: "Because there is a surplus of available workers in Skagit County, new business and industry are eligible for state tax credits". Under financial programs it states: "Low interest loans are available to new industry creating jobs in Skagit County. Average hourly wages range from $4 to $9". Would the Member comment on that? Is that the kind of competition the Member would like to see in terms of the B.C. processing industry? Would the Hon. Member agree that British Columbians have a fundamental right to eviscerate fish? Many of our trading partners, such as France and Great Britain, will not allow

British Columbia salmon into their markets unless it is eviscerated.
No one, including the Americans, has ever gone to GATT to challenge the right of a country to demand that incoming British Columbian and Canadian product be eviscerated. Do we have a right to do that? Does the Hon. Member see what the real design is here?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the Hon. Member from Skeena and I have much in common in that we both, you might say, represent border areas and we both have fish processing plants in our ridings. We should remind ourselves that it was because of the highly competitive nature of the plants in the Prince Rupert area that we were buying fish from southern Alaska that really upset the Americans. In other words, the Canadian fish plants with their modem processing and excellent workforce were able to buy American fish and process them. The American processors were unable to get the fish for their plants.
As far as my own area is concerned, we do have several fish processing plants. These are all new plants. They are well equipped and I have not had any complaints from any of their people about the possibility of heading south. In fact, I think they are all looking for more sources of fish. They are looking for areas where they can get more fish rather than worrying about moving south.
As far as the letter from Skagit County to processors is concerned, I think this is fairly routine. I can show you several letters from my own municipality of Delta. Letters have been sent to other businesses encouraging them to come to Delta, telling them all about the virtues of the place. I have not heard concerns from people in the fish plants in my area that they are seriously considering a move south. Right now, the processors have ready access to fish and I cannot see that this is a factor.
I used to work in the Prince Rupert Cold Storage many years ago. It was mentioned earlier about the trucking of fish to the States. At that time all kinds of fish were being transported via reefer barges through Prince Rupert to Seattle and to Vancouver. I think this whole industry is highly mobile and as long as our plants can remain competitive, keep up to date and produce a top quality product, we do not have too much to be concerned about.
The second part of the Member's question concerned evisceration. I think we all recognize that if you do not eviscerate the fish as soon as possible, it deteriorates. This has been recognized by Canadian officials and is why they want these landing requirements. If fish are landed and reloaded again with the guts left in, as time passes the quality will deteriorate. I think if we can get these landing requirements through, and I have every reason to believe they will because they have been judged to be GATT-consistent, then I trust we can have these fish completely processed. I would like to see them smoked, canned and whatever else we can do to have value added. It is important for British Columbia.

Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to the speech by the Hon. Member for Delta (Mr. Wilbee) and also to the reply he just gave the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton). Madam Speaker, I think the Hon. Member's speech should provide the people of British Columbia with some measure of reassurance regarding the Government's intentions. I think it also puts the debate in a more logical context, allowing for market conditions and for the ability and expertise of the people of British Columbia which, with the Government's support, should help get them through the present situation.
I would like to direct the following question to the Hon. Member for Delta, and perhaps he could inform the House how he expects the fish processing plants in his riding in British Columbia to remain competitive with processing plants in the United States.

Madam Speaker, there are great changes going on in the fishing industry with the fish farms and so on. A few years ago there used to be canneries all over the coast. Changes in the ability to transport fish with the modem seiners and gill netters make it possible to cool the product right away. Before, they had to unload it every day. They can now go for several days with icing. This is even in the smaller ships.
What this has done, of course, is tremendously increase the quality of the fish that are available. It is still a fact that the sooner fish is processed, the better the quality.
June 15, 1989

We talked about the Japanese market earlier. I think this is a wide-open field for us to go into. Top quality, well prepared sea food. The market is going to be unlimited. This is where the plants in my area are concentrating. They are going into the Japanese markets as well as trying to maintain their nick in the European and North American markets.
I think because we are closest to the source of the fish, we have the best fish. They can be brought in and processed rapidly under ideal conditions. We have an edge on quality. The workforce that we have is highly skilled. We have an excellent marketing program. I think this is what is going to maintain the fishing industry in British Columbia.

Madam Speaker, I want to say a few words on this motion which is very ably worded by the NDP. I congratulate them for bringing it forth and in such an imaginative way. It allows people to put their seats on the line. It shows how strongly they feel about it.
The reason I want to stand up and say a few words is because we feel just as strongly. This is an issue that is not confined to one coast.
We had a visit on Wednesday in the Atlantic Liberal caucus from the consortium who put together this trip, and this initiative, and this exercise called "The case for government action to protect and develop the fishing industry". It included the United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union. We have those in my province and in the Atlantic provinces as well. The Prince Rupert Amalgamated Shoreworkers and Clerks Union and others were included. They came to us as people from the West Coast and people from the East Coast with a handout for help in a situation that affects us all.
Whether people live on the East Coast of Canada or the West Coast of Canada, they are a coastal people. The reason we live there is the marine resource. We live by the sea and from the sea. We live off the sea. If the harvest of the sea is threatened, then it threatens us on both coasts. We understand the seriousness of that.
Indeed in their brief and documents they put together, they suggest that both coasts are at risk. The document says that Canada is the world's largest fish exporter, but
4,000	B.C. shore workers and an equal number in the Maritimes face lay-offs while unprocessed fish move
Supply
south. Our greatest export industry, the mainstay of our coastal economy, is at stake if we fail to act.
Let us look at the B.C. situation first. We are told that the Government could have done nothing, yet I think my colleague from Winnipeg said earlier today that they could have acted. They could have acted and refused to act. Indeed as the Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) has pointed out, the issue has been fudged all along. They could have fought, in the Free Trade Agreement, for the protection of the West Coast fishery as they did for the Atlantic. They could have insisted that it be on the table, but they did not. They let that go by. They put it on the table as a bargaining chip. They gave it up. It was a give-away on behalf of the Government of Canada. They must be held to account for that.
Second, they could have vetoed the GATT ruling. My understanding is that Canada had the right to veto the GATT ruling when it was made, yet it decided not to. The Government did not veto the ruling. Instead, it attempted to implement regulations to ensure that fish were landed, graded, and eviscerated in Canada. Those regulations are not going to hold up.
What these regulations do and what the actions of the Government of Canada do are to put the fishermen and plant workers on the West Coast of Canada on the same footing as those in the United States. The fishing industry in the United States now has the same equal opportunity to Canadian fish as do Canadian fishermen and Canadian plants.
What has really happened is that we have given up our sovereign right to develop our own natural resource.
I want to point out that we can talk all we like about the changing market-place and changing economy. The fact is that on both coasts, we are still a resource-based economy. There are not the alternatives that are available in parts of central Canada and other parts of the country. The East and West Coasts are still resource-based economies. What Canada has now done is to give up our right to control the harvest of the sea.
I think the Government has to be held to account for that, because there will not be equality. Americans and Canadians are not on the same footing. The fact is that in the U.S., there are lower wages. In the U.S., there are no medicare costs. In the U.S., there is no national unemployment insurance program. That means that the U.S. is in a better position to compete for Canadian fish than our Canadian plants. We are going to see jobs going

to the U.S. We are going to see jobs going to the U.S. on the West Coast just as we are for the East Coast.
The brief that was put together by the West Coast people points out very vividly and very graphically that the Atlantic coast is at risk as well.
My colleague from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception was criticized by the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) this afternoon for focusing on the Atlantic coast. As I pointed out earlier and as is pointed out in this brief, this is not simply a West Coast issue. The West Coast is at risk right now. The West Coast is concerned. The West Coast is threatened. The Atlantic is no less threatened. Our turn will come. This brief points out that the future of our coastal communities is threatened by the Government's apparent inability to protect and manage our marine resources. All four maritime provinces have long had legislation giving them the right to control or eliminate the export of unprocessed fish. This legislation was grandfathered into the Free Trade Agreement. Similar regulations protecting B.C.'s salmon and herring were specifically excluded.
It was a short-lived victory for the maritime industry because it is at risk too. Many of our products will be at risk. The implications for the Atlantic fishing industry are clear.
The Member for Skeena referred to Article 12.03 of the Free Trade Agreement. There is nothing to prevent the U.S. from challenging the Atlantic statutes in the GATT. The Tory Government has, in effect, conceded that we do not have the right to restrict the export of unprocessed fish in order to protect jobs on the West Coast. The same applies to the East Coast because the Government has treated us in the same way.
This afternoon, the Government and Minister for Trade claimed that the overriding principle behind the actions of the Government is to respond to protectionism in the United States. They were afraid of what would happen. They were afraid of the threat from the U.S. if we did not sign the Free Trade Agreement. That is the overriding principle. We had to do it. We had no choice. We had no option. We had to operate within GATT. We cannot exclude ourselves from GATT. We cannot ignore
GATT. We cannot challenge GATT. We cannot overrule GATT. We cannot veto GATT.
That is what the Minister of Trade said this afternoon. That is the underlying principle behind the actions of the Government. Surely, there is a more important principle. That is the sovereign right of Canada to harvest and manage its own resources for its own people. Surely that is a more fundamental principle. If we give up that principle, we are really giving up our nationhood and sovereignty as Canadians. I submit that that is the underlying principle.
The Government has caved in to American interests. We are suffering the consequences. What are the alternatives? Has the Government thought about that? What is going to happen to those people?
Nobody has lost their jobs yet. The Minister of Trade admitted this afternoon that they could. Maybe fishermen will not lose their jobs, but plant workers may. The Minister of Trade admitted that in the House this afternoon.
What are the alternatives? I can tell you that on the East Coast there are no alternatives. The fishing industry is the mainstay of our economy. Why are there
500,000	people in my province yet millions of Newfoundlanders spread across the country? Why are they in Ttiktoyaktuk, Thompson, Manitoba and Galt, Ontario. Why are they in Toronto? Why are they in other parts of the country? They are there because the jobs are there. They have been forced to go to those places to look for work. Now, with the crisis in the fish stocks off the East Coast, there will be more people going down the road.
At the same time, the Canadian social security system is beginning to be dismantled. Today we were having a debate in Question Period and the main theme was the unemployment insurance program. We have had that safety net to fall back on. It has not been available to the Americans, but we have had it here and we can be proud of the social security system that we have had.
At the same time as the fishing industry is in crisis on the West and East Coast, at the same time that jobs are threatened in the fishing industry on the West and East Coast, at the same time where there are very few, if any, alternatives for employment on those coasts, the Government is starting to dismantle the Canadian social security system.

Under unemployment insurance a person will receive less benefits and have to work for more weeks in order to quality, and will have to pay more premiums. With the money that it gains, the Government is going to start to train people. It will not provide jobs, but it will train people.
For what will the Government train a 40 year-old fisherman who lives in a small community of about 500 on an isolated coast? He is going to lose his job. His children are the ones who will be affected. His wife is the one who will suffer. His community will suffer. The Government states it is going to stop paying those social security payments to people who are out of work through no fault of their own and it is going to train them. For what is the Government going to train that fisherman whose livelihood is affected, and whose family's livelihood is affected as a result of the negligence of the Government?
It is a myth, and an idea that has jumped full blown from the vivid imagination of some central Canadian bureaucrat. It does not make any sense at all. The management policy does not make any sense, and the social security policy does not make any sense for both the West Coast and East Coast. Whose interests are being served, I do not know, but it is not the people who live on either coast. Those are the implications of what has happened.
This Government prefers to let market forces govern no matter what, and particularly if those market forces originate in the United States. In this country we are falling into a master/slave relationship with the United States. Someone today stated that we are starting to become second-class citizens in our own country. That is what is happening.

That is what is happening as a result of the GATT ruling. That is what is happening as a result of the free
